items.title: The damped driven oscillator model: second-order equation, phase-plane system and characteristic data
items.statement: The damped driven oscillator model m x''+c x'+k x=f(t) with m>0, c>=0, k real, f continuous; its phase-plane system G_f(t,x,v)=(v,(f(t)-c v-k x)/m); the characteristic polynomial, discriminant, damping rate, undamped and damped frequencies; equilibria and the local Lipschitz property. No physical interpretation is asserted.
items.strategy: Define the model, its solution notion, the phase-plane reduction and the characteristic data with explicit domains and regularity; no existence or uniqueness claim is smuggled into the definition.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.13a): harmonic oscillator, linear drag force, damping coefficient and the forced equation $m\ddot q+\eta\dot q+\kappa q=F(t)$; printed pages 1-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.15): the linearised forced damped oscillator and the underdamped, critically damped and overdamped solution cases, printed pages 147-148

items.title: Periodic averaging data: the average field, the oscillatory part and the periodic deviation
items.statement: For continuous, state-C1, P-periodic f: the average f-bar, the oscillatory part f-f-bar, the periodic deviation g(t,x)=int_0^t(f-f-bar) with its unique P-periodic extension, and the averaged system y'=epsilon f-bar(y).
items.strategy: Introduce the averaging objects by explicit formulas and state the periodic extension's well-definedness conditions; all bounds are proved separately.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): harmonic balance and the reduced (RWA) equations obtained by time averaging over one period, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.25)-(5.28): averaging the first-order perturbation over one period and the secular change of the averaged variable, printed pages 95-98

items.title: A one-frequency parameter-dependent action-angle branch, its transformed Hamiltonian and its drift generator
items.statement: A one-frequency parameter-dependent action-angle datum: C2 functions h,k with k 2pi-periodic in theta, the transformed Hamiltonian K=h+epsilon k, the frequency omega=partial_I h, the angle average, the drift generator g=(k-<k>)/omega, and the branch vector field (I,theta,s)'=(-epsilon partial_theta k, partial_I h+epsilon partial_I k, epsilon).
items.strategy: Define the branch datum, its drift generator and its vector field explicitly; the existence of such a chart for a given family is left as a consumer hypothesis.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.149)-(4.158): the action $I=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$ of a one-dimensional family with slow parameter $\lambda(t)$ and the averaged statement $\langle\dot I\rangle=0$, printed pages 113-115

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): action variable $J=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$, the averaged energy-change identity and the adiabatic-invariance conclusion $J=\text{const}$, printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244)

items.title: Differentiation of a variable-limit convolution integral with a C-one matrix kernel
items.reference: batch-7-local-construction; a necessary mathematical prerequisite added by this scaffolder and recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: For a C1 matrix kernel g and continuous f on an interval I with base point t0, the map t -> int_{t0}^t g(t-s) f(s) ds is differentiable (indeed C1 when g is C2) on the interior of I, with derivative g(0)f(t)+int_{t0}^t g'(t-s)f(s)ds.
items.strategy: Split the difference quotient into a parameter-derivative term over a fixed interval, handled by differentiation under the integral sign, and a moving-endpoint term, handled by uniform continuity; then prove continuity of the derivative.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Sections 3.1-3.2: the matrix exponential, linear systems and the variation-of-constants formula for $\dot x=A(t)x+f(t)$, printed pages 57-66
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Section 8.4 (the second fundamental theorem of calculus and differentiation of parameter integrals), online text

items.title: The homogeneous damped oscillator: solution classification by the discriminant and uniqueness for initial data
items.statement: For m>0, c>=0, k>0 the solutions of m x''+c x'+k x=0 are exactly the restrictions of the three families determined by the sign of Delta=c^2-4mk (distinct real roots, double root with the factor t, and e^{-gamma t}(A cos omega t+B sin omega t)); for every initial datum there is exactly one global solution, with explicit coefficient formulas.
items.strategy: Verify each family by direct differentiation (using the complex exponential in the oscillatory case), match initial data by explicit linear algebra, and prove exhaustiveness by a connectedness argument using the local uniqueness lemma for the phase-plane field.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.6)-(5.12): characteristic equation $\lambda^2+2\delta\lambda+\omega_0^2=0$, its roots (5.8) and the free solution (5.9); printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): underdamped, critically damped and overdamped solution cases of the linearised oscillator, printed page 148

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 3.2 and Section 3.7 (linear systems and the harmonic oscillator), printed pages 60-66 and 87-89

items.title: The degenerate and repulsive oscillator: solutions for k=0 and the explicit growing solution for k<0
items.statement: For k=0 the solutions of m x''+c x'=0 are A+B e^{-ct/m} (c>0) and A+Bt (c=0); for k<0 the roots lambda_+>0>lambda_- are real and the solutions are A e^{lambda_+t}+B e^{lambda_-t}, so e^{lambda_+t} is an unbounded solution on [0,infinity).
items.strategy: Derive the k=0 families by integrating the first-order equation for x'; verify the exponential solutions for k<0, exhibit the growing solution, and obtain uniqueness from the local uniqueness lemma.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.6)-(5.9): characteristic equation and the free damped solutions, including the high-damping and free cases, printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16) and the surrounding classification of linearised oscillator solutions, printed page 148

items.title: Variation of constants for $z'=Az+b(t)$ via the matrix exponential
items.statement: For A in M_n(R), continuous b and data (t0,z0), the map z(t)=E(t-t0)z0+int_{t0}^t E(t-s)b(s)ds with E the matrix exponential is the unique solution of z'=Az+b on every interval containing t0; E is C1, E(u+v)=E(u)E(v), E'=AE=EA and ||E(u)||<=e^{||A|| |u|}.
items.strategy: Combine the exponential-series lemma with the convolution differentiation lemma to verify the explicit solution, and prove uniqueness by Gronwall.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 3.1 (the matrix exponential, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.4) and Section 3.2 (the inhomogeneous linear system $\dot x=A(t)x+f(t)$, variation of constants), printed pages 57-66

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.27)-(5.30): the temporal Green's function as the response to a short pulse, $q(t)=\int f(t')G(t-t')\,dt'$, printed pages 6-7 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 92-93)

items.title: Strictly damped homogeneous oscillator with $k>0$: every solution tends to zero
items.statement: For m>0, c>0, k>0 every solution of the homogeneous model tends to 0 as t->+infinity, with the explicit bounds |x(t)|<=(|A|+|B|)e^{lambda_+ t}, |x(t)|<=(|A|+|B|t)e^{lambda t}, |x(t)|<=(|A|+|B|)e^{-gamma t} in the three discriminant cases.
items.strategy: Read the three explicit families off the classification theorem, bound them by the sign of the roots and the range of sine and cosine, and take the limits (including the t e^{lambda t} case by an exponential-series lower bound).

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.9)-(5.12): exponential decay of the free damped oscillations with time constant $\tau=1/\delta$ and the quality factor, printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): the transient term of the linearised oscillator decays away exponentially, printed page 148

items.title: The forced oscillator with $k\ge0$: unique global solution and the convolution (Green's function) formula
items.statement: For m>0, c>=0, k>=0 and continuous f on an interval I, the forced model has exactly one solution on I for every initial datum, and it equals a homogeneous solution plus the convolution int_{t0}^t g(t-s)f(s)ds with g the homogeneous kernel g(0)=0, g'(0)=1/m; the explicit kernel is recorded in the remarks.
items.strategy: Construct the solution as homogeneous part plus convolution, verify the equation by two applications of the convolution lemma using g''=-(c g'+k g)/m, and invoke the variation-of-constants uniqueness.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.13)-(5.18) and (5.27)-(5.30): the forced equation, the response function and the temporal Green's function $q(t)=\int f(t')G(t-t')\,dt'$, printed pages 3-7 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 89-93)

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 3.2 (variation of constants for inhomogeneous linear systems) and Section 8.6 (forced harmonic oscillator), printed pages 60-66 and 224-230

items.title: Forced quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=\varphi(t)$: decoupled forced modes and the convolution solution
items.statement: For symmetric positive definite M and symmetric non-negative K the forced system M q''+K q=phi(t) decouples under z=O^T M^{1/2}q into z_i''+lambda_i z_i=psi_i, and each scalar mode is solved by the explicit convolution formula (sin kernel when lambda_i>0, ramp kernel when lambda_i=0); the solution for every initial datum is unique.
items.strategy: Transport the forced system through the modal transformation of the quadratic-mode theorem and apply the scalar forced-oscillator theorem mode by mode.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 8.6, formulas (8.76)-(8.81): decoupled harmonic modes of $Mq''+Wq=0$ and their energies; Section 3.2 for the inhomogeneous linear solution structure
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 2.6 (normal modes and their equations), printed pages 40-45

items.title: Sinusoidal forcing: the steady response, its amplitude and phase, and resonance at $\Omega=\sqrt{k/m}$
items.statement: For f(t)=f0 cos(Omega t): if D=k-m Omega^2+i c Omega is nonzero, x_p=Re(f0 e^{i Omega t}/D) is an exact solution with the displayed real form and amplitude |f0|/sqrt(D modulus^2); if c=0 and Omega=omega_0 then x_p=f0 t sin(omega_0 t)/(2m omega_0) solves the equation and is unbounded for f0 nonzero; if c>0 every solution equals x_p plus a homogeneous solution, so the transient decays and the solution is bounded.
items.strategy: Verify the complex ansatz and take real parts, verify the resonant solution directly and exhibit its unbounded sequence, and use the linear splitting plus the homogeneous decay corollary for the transient statement.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.14)-(5.22): the response function, the forced amplitude (5.18), the resonance value (5.19) and the resonance discussion, printed pages 3-5 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 89-91)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eqs. (7.15)-(7.16): transient plus steady state forced motion with resonant behaviour at drive frequency equal to the natural frequency, printed pages 147-148

items.title: The amplitude of the sinusoidally forced damped oscillator: location and value of its maximum
items.statement: For c>0 the amplitude A(Omega)=|f0|/sqrt((k-m Omega^2)^2+c^2 Omega^2) is strictly increasing then strictly decreasing with maximum at Omega_*=sqrt(k/m-c^2/(2m^2)) when c^2<2mk and maximum at Omega=0 otherwise; the maximum value is 2m|f0|/(c sqrt(4mk-c^2)) in the first case.
items.strategy: Write the denominator as an exact square m^2(u-u_*)^2+c^2(4mk-c^2)/(4m^2) in u=Omega^2, locate the vertex, and convert the monotonicity through the strictly decreasing maps x->1/x and x->sqrt(x).

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.18)-(5.22) and Fig. 5.1: the forced amplitude and the resonance peak, printed pages 4-5 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 90-91)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3: 'the steady state forced motion (whose amplitude exhibits resonant behavior at omega_D = 1)', printed page 148

items.title: Elementary bounds for the periodic average, the deviation and its time derivative
items.reference: batch-7-local-construction; a necessary mathematical prerequisite added by this scaffolder and recorded in the batch notes
items.statement: In the averaging setting with |f|<=M and state-Lipschitz constant L on a ball: |f-bar|<=M and f-bar is L-Lipschitz; |g|<=2MP and g is 2LP-Lipschitz in x; partial_t g=f-f-bar everywhere; and D_x g(t,x)=int_0^t(D_x f-D_x f-bar)ds with ||D_x g||<=2LP, so g is totally differentiable.
items.strategy: Estimate the integrals with the norm inequality and monotonicity, control the time derivative by the fundamental theorem and periodicity at multiples of P, and obtain the state derivative by differentiation under the integral sign.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): time averaging over one period and the reduced equations, with the first-order-order-of-magnitude bookkeeping, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.25)-(5.28): average over one period and size of the oscillatory versus secular parts, printed pages 95-98

items.title: Finite-time linearization error bound: quadratic remainder, exponential growth bound and the variation-of-constants estimate
items.statement: For F continuous and locally Lipschitz with ||F(z)-Az||<=C||z||^2 and ||F(z)||<=L||z|| on the ball of radius r, every datum with delta e^{LT}<r gives a solution z on [0,T] with ||z(t)||<=delta e^{Lt}, and ||z(t)-y(t)||<=C delta^2 int_0^t e^{||A||(t-s)}e^{2Ls}ds <= C delta^2 t e^{(||A||+2L)t}, where y solves y'=Ay.
items.strategy: Bound the maximal solution by Gronwall while it stays in the ball, extend it to [0,T] by compact continuation, and compare it with the linear solution by the variation-of-constants formula.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.4 (Theorem 2.10, smooth dependence and the first variational equation) and Sections 6.2-6.3 (linearisation and stability estimates), printed pages 45-48 and 192-197

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3: the linearised version of the damped oscillator and the limits of linear reasoning, printed pages 147-148

items.title: Averaging for fast periodic oscillations: order-$\varepsilon$ agreement on the $O(1/\varepsilon)$ time scale
items.statement: If the averaged solution y stays in the ball of radius R-rho on [0,A/epsilon] and epsilon K<rho with K=e^{LA}[B+(LB+B1 M)A], B=2MP, B1=2LP, then the solution x of x'=epsilon f(t,x) exists on [0,A/epsilon] and ||x(t)-y(t)||<=epsilon K there.
items.strategy: Conjugate x by the deviation g to cancel the oscillatory term exactly, apply Gronwall to the resulting difference with y, and use the smallness condition to prevent exit from the trapping ball.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): the reduced (averaged) equations for a weakly perturbed oscillator, obtained to first order in the small parameter, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.22)-(5.28): splitting a perturbation into periodic and secular parts and averaging over one period, printed pages 96-98

items.title: Adiabatic action drift bound: order-$\varepsilon$ change of the action on the $O(1/\varepsilon)$ time scale
items.statement: For a C2 action-angle branch with |partial_I h|>=omega_0>0 on compact sets K x S0 and a branch solution staying there, |I(t)-I(0)|<=epsilon[2 sup|g| + A sup|partial_I g partial_theta k - partial_theta g partial_I k - partial_s g|] on [0,A/epsilon].
items.strategy: Compute the exact chain-rule identity (I+epsilon g)'=epsilon^2(partial_I g partial_theta k - partial_theta g partial_I k - partial_s g), integrate it over the horizon, and bound the two error terms.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): the adiabatic regime, the averaged energy-change identity and the invariance of the action variable to the accuracy of the averaged argument, printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244)

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.148)-(4.158): the averaged statement $\langle\dot I\rangle=0$ for a slowly varying parameter, with the author's explicit note that more rigorous proofs exist elsewhere, printed pages 113-115

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.23)-(5.28): secular versus periodic first-order effects after averaging over one period, printed pages 96-98

items.title: Scope and limits of the oscillator, linearization, averaging and adiabatic items on this page
items.statement: A scope remark separating the exact oscillator classification and forcing statements from the approximate ones: the linearization bound is finite-time and conditional on delta e^{LT}<r; averaging compares two models on an O(1/epsilon) horizon; the adiabatic bound needs a uniform chart with a frequency gap and trapping; no item asserts physical laws, units or empirical facts.
items.strategy: Collect the hypotheses and limits of the preceding items in one place so that consumers carry them; no proof obligation is discharged by the remark.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Sections 5.1 and 5.3 and Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3: the perturbative and averaged character of the oscillator, reduced-equation and adiabatic discussion

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6: the author's explicit remark that the intuitive adiabatic argument is approximate and that stricter proofs exist elsewhere

items.title: Five worked initial value problems for the homogeneous oscillator in the four discriminant cases
items.statement: Five worked initial value problems: x''+4x=0 with cos 2t; x''+2x'+x=0 with (1-t)e^{-t}; x''+3x'+x=0 with the two-exponential solution; x''+2x'=0 with (1-e^{-2t})/2; and x''-x=0 with the unbounded cosh solution.
items.strategy: Compute the discriminant and coefficients from the classification theorem and the degenerate-case proposition and check the initial data explicitly.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.2)-(5.9): the free oscillator solution in the undamped, damped and high-damping cases, printed pages 1-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): underdamped, critically damped and overdamped classification of the linearised oscillator, printed page 148

items.title: Resonant forcing at $\Omega=\omega_0$ and the two regimes of the amplitude maximum
items.statement: The resonant solution x_p=(1/2) t sin t of x''+x=cos t and its unboundedness; the amplitude maximum at Omega_*=1/sqrt2 with value 2/sqrt3 for c=1; and the maximum at Omega=0 for c=2, with A(1)=1/2.
items.strategy: Substitute the resonant candidate using sine and cosine derivatives and evaluate the amplitude formula in the two regimes.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.18)-(5.22): the resonance peak, the value (5.19) at $\omega=\omega_0$ and the FWHM (5.20), printed pages 4-5 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 90-91)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): steady state forced motion with resonant behaviour at the drive frequency, printed page 148

items.title: Constant forcing: free fall and the approach to terminal velocity under linear drag
items.statement: The constant-forcing solutions x=x0+v0 t+g t^2/2 (zero stiffness and damping) and x=t/2-(1-e^{-2t})/4 for x''+2x'=1 from rest, with velocity approaching the terminal value 1/2.
items.strategy: Read the solutions from the convolution representation with the explicit homogeneous kernels and differentiate.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eq. (5.13) and Chapter 2 Section 2.4 (linear drag and terminal velocity in one-dimensional motion), printed pages 3 and 2-4 of the respective chapters
I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1: the damped oscillator equation and its damping parameter, printed pages 146-148

items.title: Finite-time linearization bound for the planar pendulum with explicit constants
items.statement: For the pendulum field F(theta,omega)=(omega,-sin theta): the remainder bound with C=1/12 and growth constant L=sqrt2 on the ball of radius 1/2, and the resulting linearization error below 10^{-4} for delta=1/100 on [0,1].
items.strategy: Bound |sin theta - theta| by the Taylor remainder and |F(z)| by the norm of z, then substitute into the linearization theorem with ||A||=1.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 6.3 (linearisation estimates) and Theorem 2.10, printed pages 45-48 and 192-197

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3: the linearised oscillator equation and the role of the nonlinear term, printed pages 147-148

items.title: Averaging estimate on $[0,100]$ for the scalar equation $x'=\varepsilon\cos t$
items.statement: For f(t,x)=cos t: f-bar=0, g=sin t, B=4pi, B1=0, K=4pi; with epsilon=1/100 the theorem gives |x(t)|<=pi/25 on [0,100] while the exact solution is (1/100) sin t.
items.strategy: Evaluate the averaging data and constants, verify the trapping hypotheses, and compare the theorem's bound with the exact solution.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): first-order averaging of a fast periodic term, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.25)-(5.26): a perturbation whose one-period average vanishes produces only a periodic change, printed pages 96-97

items.title: An exactly solvable adiabatic branch: $K=I+\varepsilon I\cos\theta$ and comparison with the drift bound
items.statement: For h=I, k=I cos theta, epsilon=0.1: the exact invariant I(1+0.1 cos theta), trapping in [1.2,1.9], the exact drift bound 1/3, and the theorem's value 19/50.
items.strategy: Exhibit the exact invariant of the branch system, verify trapping, and evaluate the theorem's constant (whose A-dependent term vanishes identically here).

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): action variable and adiabatic invariance, printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244)

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.150)-(4.158): the action $I=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$ and the averaged invariance statement, printed pages 113-115

items.title: Continuity alone does not give uniqueness: $x'=\sqrt{|x|}$ through the origin
items.statement: The continuous field F(x)=sqrt(|x|) admits both the zero solution and x_1(t)=0 for t<=1, (t-1)^2/4 for t>=1 through x(0)=0, so continuity alone does not imply uniqueness; F is not locally Lipschitz at 0.
items.strategy: Verify both solutions directly and conclude that the refuted uniqueness statement fails.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.2 (the Picard iteration and the role of the Lipschitz hypothesis; examples of nonunique solutions), printed pages 25-32

J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.2 (existence and uniqueness statements and the necessity of a Lipschitz condition), printed pages 12-21

items.title: A bounded field whose solution leaves the domain in finite time: $x'=v$, $v'=0$ on $(0,\infty)\times(-2,2)$
items.statement: For F(x,v)=(v,0) on the domain (0,infinity) x (-2,2), the solution through (1,-1) is (1-t,-1) with maximal interval (-infinity,1): the solution reaches the excluded boundary at t=1 although ||F(x,v)||=|v|<2 is bounded on its entire domain, so boundedness alone does not give global existence.
items.strategy: Verify the explicit solution and show that no extension past t=1 can meet the domain condition.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.1 and the blow-up examples of Chapter 2 (maximal domains are determined by the open domain of the field, not only by the size of the field), printed pages 17-24
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.3 (maximal solutions and the role of the domain boundary), printed pages 22-30
